newsitem.title: USA: NFL-MINISTER OF DEFENSE USES SUPER BOWL AS PULPIT.
newsitem.headline: NFL-MINISTER OF DEFENSE USES SUPER BOWL AS PULPIT.

text.p: Green Bay Packers defensive end Reggie White, an ordained minister whose other job is terrorising opposing quarterbacks, is using the Super Bowl stage as his pulpit this week.
After 12 brilliant National Football League seasons with Philadelphia and Green Bay, White is finally no longer in danger of being considered the best player never to make it to the Super Bowl.
On Sunday against the New England Patriots in Super Bowl XXXI, the future Hall of Famer will finally live his dream of playing for a championship.
And while his excitement over the long-awaited title shot is obvious, White has seized the opportunity to address the media masses on issues he considers more important than football.

"It may get on you guys' nerves," he said about preaching his spiritual beliefs, "but if I can change one person by what I'm saying, if one person can hear me today and their life changes, than getting to (Patriots quarterback Drew) Bledsoe don't make no difference.
"Reggie White cares about people," he said. "I want to be a leader not only to the black community but to all communities."
Green Bay head coach Mike Holmgren says White is genuinely out to make the world a better place as well as make the Packers Super Bowl winners.

"I think it's common knowledge what a great person Reggie is. I have said many times he is the real thing. There is no flim-flam there," Holmgren said of the 11-time Pro Bowl selection, who goes by the nickname "Minister of Defence."
A striking figure at 6-foot-5 (1.95 m) and 300 pounds (136 kg), White can seem almost angelic when discussing his religion and his desire to help people.
He can also breathe fire and brimstone when the subject turns to racism and a rash of church burnings in the United States that has touched him personally.
And it's not just talk for the man who was named to the NFL's 75th anniversary all-time team.
He is involved in all manner of philanthropic and community programmes, from helping people to get off welfare to assisting with the start-up of small businesses in the inner cities.
"We're teaching people responsiblility, not just giving away money," he said Thursday in his last sermon to the media before the big game.

The 35-year-old White claims that when he became the league's most prized free agent four years ago, God sent him to the Packers to win a Super Bowl. He admitted that Green Bay, with its practically non-existent black population, seemed an unlikely destination for him.
"My brother-in-law is this tall," he said, gesturing at his waist level, "and people think that (because he is black) he plays for the Packers," he said laughing.
"We're they're heroes, but sometimes it gets irritating."
Still White is impressed by the love he feels from the fans and residents of Green Bay.
He was especially moved when Wisconsin residents donated more than $200,000 to help rebuild his Knoxville, Tennessee, church after it was torched last year.

"That just convinced me of how great the people were up there. That said to me, 'Reggie White we believe in you,' it did something to me and my wife that's never been done before," said White, who is planning to set up permanent residence in Wisconsin.
"To me there's not a lot of progress been made with these churches because churches are still burning down," he said angrily earlier this week.
White said FBI agents complained to him that some black people were not cooperating with their investigation.
"My thing is how do you expect black people to accept you when the name of the FBI building is the Hoover building.
"How do you expect people to accept knowing that this man (former FBI director J. Edgar Hoover) was a known racist."
He also bristles at the idea that the NFL would like to curtail open displays of prayer on the field.
"We're not forcing our prayers on anyone.
"They don't want us to do the things that Dennis Rodman does. They want us to be role models.... The league should be impressed that we're humbling ourselves to a higher being."
The rhetoric tones down and another type of passion enters the minister's voice when the subject turns to the ultimate football game, just three days away, and how badly he wants to win it.
"I've never been this far. It's the last opportunity that a lot of us may have and we definitely want to take advantage of it," he said.
He insisted that Green Bay's longing to return to the great championship days of the 1960s added incentive, rather than pressure to these Packers.
"Because of the tradition, I told our guys the first year I was here, if you win a championship in Green Bay it will be unlike anything else in the world."
